chapter.name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
chapter.blurb: The chapter classifies solids as metals, semiconductors and insulators by conductivity and by energy bands, and explains conduction in pure (intrinsic) and doped (n-type and p-type) semiconductors through electrons and holes. It then describes how a p-n junction forms, with its depletion region and barrier potential, and how a junction diode behaves under forward and reverse bias. Finally it applies the diode as a half-wave and a full-wave rectifier with a capacitor filter.

concepts.name: Classification of metals, semiconductors and insulators
concepts.description: Classifying solids by their conductivity or resistivity and by their energy bands: valence band, conduction band and the energy gap between them.
concepts.idea: Whether a solid is a metal, a semiconductor or an insulator is decided by how its valence band and conduction band are placed: overlapping (or partly filled), separated by a small gap, or separated by a large gap.
concepts.rule: By conductivity (indicative ranges): metals have resistivity about 10^-2 to 10^-8 ohm m (conductivity 10^2 to 10^8 S/m); semiconductors about 10^-5 to 10^6 ohm m (10^5 to 10^-6 S/m); insulators about 10^11 to 10^19 ohm m (10^-11 to 10^-19 S/m), with resistivity = 1/conductivity. Semiconductors may be elemental (Si, Ge) or compound: inorganic (CdS, GaAs, CdSe, InP), organic (anthracene, doped pthalocyanines) or organic polymers (polypyrrole, polyaniline, polythiophene). By energy bands: in a crystal the energy levels form bands. The band holding the valence electrons is the valence band; the band above it is the conduction band; the gap between the top of the valence band (E_V) and the bottom of the conduction band (E_C) is the energy gap E_g. Metals: the conduction band is partially filled, or the conduction and valence bands overlap (E_g about 0), so many electrons are available for conduction. Insulators: E_g > 3 eV, no electrons in the conduction band and thermal excitation cannot lift them there. Semiconductors: a finite but small gap, E_g < 3 eV, so at room temperature some electrons cross into the conduction band. For a Si or Ge crystal of N atoms there are 4N outer electrons and 8N available states, which split into two bands of 4N states each; at absolute zero the lower (valence) band is completely filled and the upper (conduction) band is completely empty.
concepts.example: A solid whose energy gap is 9 eV has no electrons in its conduction band at room temperature and is an insulator, while a solid with a gap of 0.3 eV is a semiconductor.

questions.a: First arrangement: the conduction band is partially filled and the valence band is partially empty. Electrons in a partly empty band can move from lower levels to higher vacant levels, so conduction is possible. Second arrangement: the conduction band and the valence band overlap (E_g about 0), so electrons from the valence band move easily into the conduction band and a large number of electrons become available for conduction. In both, vacant energy levels lie immediately above occupied ones with no gap to cross, so the resistance is low; in an insulator a large gap separates the filled valence band from the empty conduction band.

concepts.name: Intrinsic semiconductors: electrons and holes
concepts.description: The covalently bonded Si or Ge crystal, thermal generation of electron-hole pairs, the hole as an effective positive charge, and the electron and hole currents of a pure semiconductor.
concepts.idea: In a pure semiconductor every electron freed from a covalent bond leaves behind a hole, so electrons and holes exist in equal numbers and both carry current.
concepts.rule: Si and Ge have a diamond-like structure in which each atom is surrounded by four nearest neighbours and shares one valence electron with each, forming covalent bonds. At low temperature all bonds are intact; as temperature rises thermal energy breaks a few bonds, giving a free electron (charge -q) and a vacancy with effective charge +q called a hole. In an intrinsic semiconductor n_e = n_h = n_i, the intrinsic carrier concentration. A hole moves when a bound electron from a neighbouring bond jumps into the vacancy; the originally freed electron is not involved, and hole motion is only a convenient way of describing the motion of bound electrons. Under an electric field holes move towards the negative potential and give a hole current I_h, free electrons give an electron current I_e, and the total current is I = I_e + I_h. Generation of electron-hole pairs is accompanied by recombination (an electron colliding with a hole); at equilibrium the rate of generation equals the rate of recombination. At T = 0 K an intrinsic semiconductor behaves like an insulator; at T > 0 K thermally excited electrons partly occupy the conduction band and leave an equal number of holes in the valence band. C, Si and Ge have the same lattice structure, but their bonding electrons lie in the second, third and fourth orbits, so the energy needed to free an electron is least for Ge, more for Si and highest for C: free electrons are significant in Ge and Si and negligible in C.
concepts.example: If thermal energy breaks 12 covalent bonds in a pure crystal, 12 free electrons and 12 holes are produced, so the electron and hole numbers stay equal.

questions.q: At a fixed temperature the number of free electrons and holes in a pure semiconductor stays at a steady value instead of growing without limit, although thermal energy keeps breaking bonds. Analyse why, and state what happens to the carrier numbers when the temperature is raised.
questions.a: Two processes go on together. Generation: thermal energy breaks covalent bonds and creates electron-hole pairs. Recombination: a free electron collides with a hole and the pair is lost. As the number of carriers grows, such collisions become more frequent, until the rate of recombination equals the rate of generation; at this equilibrium the carrier numbers are steady, with n_e = n_h = n_i. When the temperature is raised more thermal energy is available, more bonds break, and equilibrium is re-established at larger but still equal numbers of electrons and holes.
s: Generation of electron-hole pairs by thermal energy and simultaneous recombination
Equilibrium when rate of generation equals rate of recombination, giving steady n_e = n_h = n_i

questions.a: At absolute zero every covalent bond is intact; in the band picture the valence band is completely filled and the conduction band is empty, so the crystal behaves like an insulator. As the temperature rises, thermal energy breaks a few bonds: each broken bond frees an electron and leaves a hole. In the band picture this is an electron excited from the valence band across the energy gap to the conduction band, leaving a hole in the valence band. At room temperature the conduction band is partly occupied by these electrons and the valence band holds an equal number of holes (n_e = n_h = n_i); both carry current, so the crystal conducts weakly.
s: 0 K: all bonds intact = valence band full, conduction band empty, behaves as an insulator
Warming: a broken bond = an electron lifted across the gap to the conduction band, leaving a hole in the valence band
Room temperature: equal numbers of electrons and holes, both conduct, conductivity small

concepts.name: Extrinsic semiconductors: doping, n-type and p-type
concepts.description: Doping a pure semiconductor with pentavalent or trivalent impurities to obtain n-type and p-type material, with their majority and minority carriers.
concepts.idea: Adding a few parts per million of a suitable impurity gives a semiconductor many extra carriers of one kind: electrons from pentavalent donors (n-type) or holes from trivalent acceptors (p-type).
concepts.rule: The conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor at room temperature is very low; adding a small amount (a few parts per million) of a suitable impurity increases it manifold. This deliberate addition is doping, the impurity atoms are dopants, and the material is an extrinsic (impurity, doped) semiconductor. The dopant must not distort the lattice, so its atoms must be nearly the same size as the semiconductor atoms; it occupies only a very few lattice sites. Pentavalent dopants (As, Sb, P): four electrons bond with the four neighbours and the fifth is very weakly bound (about 0.01 eV for Ge and 0.05 eV for Si, against about 0.72 eV and 1.1 eV to cross the forbidden band), so it is free at room temperature. The dopant is a donor; electrons are majority carriers and holes minority carriers; the material is n-type, n_e >> n_h. The number of donor electrons depends on the doping level and not on a rise in ambient temperature. Trivalent dopants (In, B, Al): the bond with the fourth neighbour has a vacancy; an electron from a neighbouring bond fills it, leaving a hole and making the dopant core negatively charged. The dopant is an acceptor, one acceptor atom gives one hole; holes are majority carriers and electrons minority carriers; the material is p-type, n_h >> n_e. The abundant majority carriers make recombination of the thermally generated minority carriers more likely, so the minority concentration falls below the intrinsic value. The crystal stays electrically neutral overall, because the charge of the additional carriers is equal and opposite to that of the ionised cores.
concepts.example: Germanium doped with antimony becomes n-type: each antimony atom gives one conduction electron and is left as a fixed positive core.

concepts.name: Energy bands of doped semiconductors and the relation n_e n_h = n_i^2
concepts.description: Donor and acceptor energy levels in the band diagram, the energy gaps of the group IV elements, and calculating electron and hole concentrations in a doped semiconductor.
concepts.idea: Doping adds an energy level very close to a band edge, so the dopants ionise easily at room temperature; the majority concentration is then fixed by the doping and the minority concentration follows from n_e n_h = n_i^2.
concepts.rule: In the band diagram of n-type Si the donor level E_D lies slightly below the bottom E_C of the conduction band (about 0.01 eV), so electrons move from it into the conduction band with a very small supply of energy. At room temperature most donor atoms are ionised but very few Si atoms are, so most conduction-band electrons come from the donors. In p-type material the acceptor level E_A lies slightly above the top E_V of the valence band (about 0.01 to 0.05 eV); an electron from the valence band jumps to E_A with very little energy (equivalently, the hole sinks from E_A into the valence band), so at room temperature most acceptors are ionised and the holes in the valence band are predominantly due to the impurity. Electrons rise up and holes fall down when they gain energy. In thermal equilibrium the electron and hole concentrations satisfy n_e n_h = n_i^2. When the doping is much larger than n_i, the majority concentration is taken equal to the dopant concentration (n_e approximately N_D for donors) and the minority concentration is n_i^2 divided by it. A doping of 1 ppm means one dopant atom per 10^6 atoms of the crystal. The different resistivities of C, Si and Ge follow from their energy gaps: 5.4 eV for C (diamond), 1.1 eV for Si and 0.7 eV for Ge; Sn, also in group IV, is a metal because its energy gap is 0 eV.
concepts.example: With n_i = 1.0 x 10^16 m^-3 and donors giving n_e = 1.0 x 10^22 m^-3, the hole concentration is n_h = (1.0 x 10^32)/(1.0 x 10^22) = 1.0 x 10^10 m^-3.

concepts.name: Formation of the p-n junction: depletion region and barrier potential
concepts.description: Diffusion and drift of carriers across a p-n junction, the depletion region of immobile ions, the junction field and the barrier potential at equilibrium.
concepts.idea: Carriers diffusing across a p-n junction uncover fixed ions that set up a field opposing further diffusion; the junction settles when the drift current balances the diffusion current.
concepts.rule: A p-n junction is made within one wafer, for example by adding a small quantity of pentavalent impurity to part of a p-Si wafer; pressing a p-type slab against an n-type slab does not work, because the surface roughness is much larger than the inter-atomic spacing (about 2 to 3 angstrom) and the contact is a discontinuity for the carriers. Because of the concentration gradient, holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side and electrons from the n-side to the p-side: this is the diffusion current. An electron leaving the n-side leaves behind an immobile ionised donor (positive); a hole leaving the p-side leaves behind an immobile ionised acceptor (negative). The positive space-charge layer on the n-side and the negative layer on the p-side together form the depletion region, about one-tenth of a micrometre thick, depleted of free charges. Its charges set up an electric field directed from the positive charge towards the negative charge (from the n-side to the p-side); this field moves electrons from the p-side to the n-side and holes from the n-side to the p-side, which is drift. The drift current is opposite to the diffusion current. At first the diffusion current is large and the drift current small; as the space-charge regions extend the field and the drift current grow until the two currents are equal, and there is then no net current. The n-material has lost electrons and the p-material has gained them, so the n-side is positive relative to the p-side; since this potential tends to prevent the movement of electrons from the n-region to the p-region it is called the barrier potential.
concepts.example: A hole wandering close to the junction on the n-side is swept by the junction field across to the p-side; this is a drift motion.

The polarity of this potential is such as to oppose the further flow of carriers by diffusion: it tends to prevent electrons moving from the n-region into the p-region (and holes from the p-region into the n-region). Because it acts as a barrier to this movement it is called the barrier potential.
s: Potential arises with the n-side positive relative to the p-side (n lost electrons, p gained them)
It opposes further movement of electrons from n to p (majority-carrier diffusion), hence 'barrier'

questions.q: When a p-n junction is formed, diffusion does not continue until the electron and hole concentrations are the same on both sides. Analyse, as a chain of cause and effect, how the junction limits its own diffusion and reaches equilibrium.
questions.a: Initially the diffusion current is large and the drift current small. Each carrier that diffuses across leaves behind an immobile ion, so the positive space charge on the n-side and the negative space charge on the p-side build up and the space-charge regions extend. This increases the strength of the electric field across the junction, and with it the drift current, which flows opposite to the diffusion current. The process continues until the drift current equals the diffusion current; there is then no net current, and a barrier potential exists across the junction that opposes further diffusion.
s: Diffusion uncovers immobile ions, so the space-charge regions extend
The junction field strengthens and the opposing drift current grows
Equilibrium when drift current equals diffusion current: no net current

questions.q: A student reasons: 'The depletion region has been emptied of charges, so there can be no electric field inside it.' Evaluate this reasoning.
questions.a: The reasoning is wrong. The depletion region is depleted only of its free (mobile) charges. It still contains immobile ionised donors (positive) on the n-side and immobile ionised acceptors (negative) on the p-side. These space charges set up an electric field directed from the positive charge towards the negative charge, that is from the n-side to the p-side.
s: Judgement - wrong; only the mobile charges are absent, immobile ionised donors and acceptors remain
These space charges produce a field from the n-side to the p-side

questions.q: Compose a description, in words, of a sketch of the electric potential plotted against position across an unbiased p-n junction, going from deep in the p-region to deep in the n-region. Say where the potential is constant, where and in which sense it changes, and what charges are responsible.
questions.a: Deep in the p-region the potential is constant, at its lower value, because that region is neutral. On entering the depletion region the potential starts to rise; it rises continuously across the depletion region, a distance of the order of one-tenth of a micrometre, passing first through the layer of negative ionised acceptors on the p-side and then through the layer of positive ionised donors on the n-side. Beyond the depletion region, deep in the n-region, it is constant again at its higher value. The total rise is the barrier potential, with the n-side positive relative to the p-side.
s: Constant (lower) potential in the neutral p-region and constant (higher) potential in the neutral n-region
Potential rises across the depletion region from the p-side to the n-side
Rise caused by negative acceptor ions on the p-side and positive donor ions on the n-side; total rise is the barrier potential

concepts.name: The semiconductor diode under forward and reverse bias
concepts.description: The p-n junction diode with an applied voltage: barrier height, depletion width and current under forward and reverse bias, the V-I characteristics and dynamic resistance.
concepts.idea: A forward bias lowers the junction barrier and gives a current of milliamperes; a reverse bias raises the barrier and leaves only a tiny, almost constant current, so the diode conducts essentially in one direction.
concepts.rule: A semiconductor diode is a p-n junction with metallic contacts at its ends, a two-terminal device; the arrow of its symbol gives the conventional direction of current under forward bias. Forward bias: p-side to the positive terminal of the battery and n-side to the negative. The applied voltage V drops mostly across the depletion region (its resistance is very high compared with the p-side and n-side) and opposes the built-in potential V0, so the depletion layer width decreases and the effective barrier height is (V0 - V). Electrons from the n-side cross to the p-side and holes from the p-side cross to the n-side, where they are minority carriers (minority carrier injection); they diffuse away from the junction, and the forward current, usually in mA, is the sum of the hole diffusion current and the conventional current due to electron diffusion. Reverse bias: n-side positive and p-side negative. The barrier height becomes (V0 + V), the depletion region widens and the diffusion current falls enormously; what remains is the drift of minority carriers swept across the junction, a current of the order of a few microampere, limited by the minority carrier concentration and not by the applied voltage. This reverse saturation current is essentially independent of voltage up to the breakdown voltage V_br, where it increases sharply; if the current exceeds the rated value the diode is destroyed by overheating. V-I characteristics are studied with a potentiometer (rheostat), a voltmeter across the diode and a milliammeter (forward bias) or microammeter (reverse bias). In forward bias the current is negligible until the threshold or cut-in voltage (about 0.2 V for a germanium diode and about 0.7 V for a silicon diode) and then rises significantly (exponentially). The forward-bias resistance is low compared with the reverse-bias resistance. Dynamic resistance r_d = (small change in voltage)/(small change in current).
concepts.example: If the forward current of a diode rises by 5 mA when the voltage across it rises by 0.05 V, its dynamic resistance is 0.05 V / 0.005 A = 10 ohm.

questions.q: In forward bias the diode current is almost negligible for small applied voltages and then rises steeply. Explain this behaviour in terms of the barrier and the energies of the carriers.
questions.a: For a small applied voltage the barrier potential is reduced only slightly below its equilibrium value, so only the small number of carriers that happen to be in the uppermost energy levels have enough energy to cross the junction, and the current is small. When the applied voltage is increased significantly the barrier height is reduced further, many more carriers have the required energy, and the current increases significantly (exponentially) for even a small further increase in voltage.
s: Small voltage: barrier only slightly reduced, only carriers in the uppermost energy levels cross, small current

questions.q: Contrast the current through a diode in forward bias with that in reverse bias under three heads: the carriers and process responsible, the typical order of magnitude, and the dependence on the applied voltage.
questions.a: Process: the forward current is due to majority carriers injected across the lowered barrier (electrons into the p-side, holes into the n-side), which then diffuse away from the junction; the reverse current is due to minority carriers that come close to the junction and are swept across it by the junction field (drift). Voltage dependence: beyond the threshold voltage the forward current rises steeply (exponentially) with voltage; the reverse current is almost independent of voltage, being limited by the minority carrier concentration, until the breakdown voltage is reached, where it increases sharply.
s: Forward: injected carriers diffusing; reverse: drift of minority carriers across the junction
Forward in mA; reverse in microampere
Forward rises steeply with voltage beyond threshold; reverse nearly constant until breakdown

If the current is not limited by the external circuit below the rated value, the diode overheats and is destroyed. General-purpose diodes are therefore not used beyond the reverse saturation current region.
s: Judgement - wrong; at breakdown the reverse current increases sharply

concepts.name: The junction diode as a rectifier
concepts.description: Half-wave and centre-tap full-wave rectifier circuits, their output waveforms and frequencies, and the capacitor filter that smooths the rectified output.
concepts.idea: Because a diode conducts only when forward biased, it passes only one half of an alternating voltage; two diodes with a centre-tap transformer use both halves, and a capacitor across the load holds the output near its peak.
concepts.rule: A rectifier is a circuit that rectifies an alternating voltage, restricting it to one direction. Half-wave rectifier: the secondary of a transformer supplies the ac across terminals A and B, and one diode is in series with the load resistor R_L. When A is positive the diode is forward biased and conducts; when A is negative it is reverse biased and does not conduct (the reverse saturation current is taken as zero). The output across R_L appears only in the positive half-cycles, so there is one output pulse per cycle and the output frequency equals the input frequency. The reverse breakdown voltage of the diode must be sufficiently higher than the peak ac voltage at the secondary. Full-wave rectifier: a centre-tap transformer and two diodes; the p-sides of the diodes are connected to the ends A and B of the secondary, the n-sides are joined, and the output is taken between this common point and the centre tap. The voltages at A and B relative to the centre tap are out of phase, so D1 conducts in one half-cycle and D2 in the other, sending current through R_L in the same direction; each diode rectifies only half the total secondary voltage. There are two output pulses per cycle, so the output frequency is twice the input frequency, and the circuit is more efficient than the half-wave rectifier. (Another full-wave circuit, needing four diodes and no centre tap, is only mentioned.) The rectified voltage is a train of half-sinusoid pulses: unidirectional but not steady. A filter makes it steady: normally a capacitor connected across the output terminals, in parallel with R_L (an inductor in series with R_L can also be used). The capacitor charges to the peak of the rectified output while the voltage rises; with no load it stays at the peak; with a load it discharges through the load and its voltage falls until it is recharged in the next half-cycle. The rate of fall depends inversely on the product C R_L, the time constant, so large capacitors are used and the output stays near the peak voltage.
concepts.example: For an ac input of 400 Hz, a half-wave rectifier gives 400 output pulses per second and a full-wave rectifier gives 800.
